items.q: Find Median from a Data Stream — the two-heaps pattern
shortAnswer: Design a class over a stream of numbers with O(log n) `addNum` and O(1) `findMedian`.
Two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half, a min-heap for the larger. Push into the left, move its max to the right, then rebalance.
Keep every left element at most every right element, with sizes within one; the median is one heap top or their average.
items.prompt:
Design a class that supports `addNum(num: Int)` and `findMedian(): Double` on a stream of numbers, with each operation O(log n) or better.

The two-heaps trick is a classic level-4 pattern: a max-heap holding the smaller half and a min-heap holding the larger half. The median is the top of one heap (odd) or the average of both tops (even). Balance invariant: the sizes may differ by at most one, and every element in the left heap ≤ every element in the right heap.
hints: The median splits the data into two halves. If you could keep the smaller half and larger half each in a structure giving their boundary elements...
A max-heap gives the *largest* of the smaller half; a min-heap gives the *smallest* of the larger half. Two heaps it is.

Insert with a two-step: push into the left heap, pop its max into the right heap, then rebalance so `left.size >= right.size` and sizes differ by ≤ 1. Kotlin's `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap — use `reverseOrder()` for the max-heap.

code.caption: Two heaps — O(log n) add, O(1) median

items.complexity: addNum is O(log n), findMedian is O(1). Space O(n). The sorted-array approach is O(n) per insert — the heaps exist precisely to buy log time.
followUps: Why push into `lo` first then move one to `hi`? Trace an ascending and a descending stream.
Now support a sliding-window median (k most recent numbers) — which heap op gets harder?
Find the k-th percentile, not just the median — generalize the heap split.

shortAnswer: Merge `k` sorted linked lists into one sorted list and return its head.
Seed a min-heap with all `k` heads, pop the smallest, append it, and push its `next` back in.
Handle null heads at seeding time and use a dummy head for the output. O(n log k) time, O(k) space — better than append-and-sort.
items.prompt:
Given a `List<ListNode?>` of k sorted singly-linked lists, merge them into one sorted list and return its head.

The naive "append all then sort" is O(n log n). The interview answer is either a priority queue over the k heads (O(n log k)) or pairwise/divide-and-conquer merging. You should be able to do the heap version fluently and name the divide-and-conquer one.
hints: At any moment the next smallest element is one of the k current heads. Which data structure returns the minimum of k candidates?
A min-heap seeded with all k heads. Pop the min, append to output, push that node's `next` back in.
Kotlin `PriorityQueue<ListNode>` needs a comparator on `value`; handle `null` heads at seeding time.

code.caption: Priority queue over k heads — O(n log k)

items.complexity: Time O(n log k) with the heap (n total nodes), O(n log n) for append-all-and-sort. Space O(k) for the heap (O(n) for sorting). The divide-and-conquer merge is O(n log k) with O(1) extra space.
followUps: Where would you put a dummy head, and why is it useful in Kotlin?
Implement the divide-and-conquer variant and compare space.
What if the k lists are not sorted? (Sort each first — the problem disappears into sort-all.)

shortAnswer: Deep-copy a linked list whose nodes also carry a `random` pointer to any node or null.
Two passes: first build a `HashMap` from each original node to its copy, then wire `next` and `random` through the map.
You can't wire `random` in one pass — its target may not exist yet. The map is O(n) space; interleaving copies gets O(1).
items.prompt:
A linked list node has `value`, `next`, and a `random` pointer that may point to any node in the list or null. Deep-copy the list: every copied node's `next` and `random` must point to copied nodes.

This is the classic "hash map first, wire pointers second" problem. Two passes: build a value copy of every node keyed by identity, then wire `next` and `random` through the map. The O(1)-space interleaving trick is the level-4 extra.
hints: You can't wire `random` on the first pass because its target may not exist yet. What do you create first?
Build all copies first in a `HashMap<Node, Node>` from original to copy — this is the O(n) space answer and it's fine to lead with it.
Second pass: `copy.next = map[orig.next]`, `copy.random = map[orig.random]`. Then mention the interleave technique (copy glued next to original) to get O(1) space.

code.caption: Map-based two-pass — O(n) time & space

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the map. The interleaved (copy glued between original nodes) version is O(n) time and O(1) extra space — mention it as the optimization, since that's what separates a level-4 answer.
followUps: Walk through the interleaving technique and its cleanup pass.
What if nodes could be shared (a DAG, not a list) — does the map approach still work?
Do the deep copy in one pass using lazy map wiring.
items.sampleCall:
run {
    val a = Node(7); val b = Node(13); val c = Node(11)
    a.next = b; b.next = c
    b.random = a; c.random = c
    val copy = copyRandomList(a)!!
    buildList { var n: Node? = copy; while (n != null) { add(n.value); n = n.next } }.toString() + " / b.random=" + copy.next!!.random!!.value
}

shortAnswer: Return whether a binary tree is a valid BST, with strict ordering at every node.
Thread an allowed `(lo, hi)` range down the recursion: tighten the high bound for left children and the low bound for right children.
The trap is checking only immediate children; ancestors constrain deeper nodes too. `Long` sentinels dodge `Int` edge-value bugs.
items.prompt:
Given the root of a binary tree, return whether it is a valid BST: for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly less, all values in its right subtree are strictly greater.

The classic trap is checking only immediate children. A node 15 with a right child 14 in a left subtree of a 20 violates the BST even though 14 < 15 and 14 < 20. The correct approach threads a (min, max) allowed range down the recursion.
hints: Checking `left < node < right` at each node is *not* enough — what global constraint is missing?
Each node has an allowed range inherited from its ancestors: (lower bound, upper bound).
Recurse with `valid(node, lo, hi)`: for the left child tighten `hi = node.value`, for the right tighten `lo = node.value`. Start with null bounds or use `Long` sentinels for values in Int range.

code.caption: Range-threading recursion — O(n)
In-order traversal must be strictly increasing

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(height) for recursion (worst case O(n) for a skewed tree). The in-order variant is O(n) time and O(height) stack too.
followUps: Why do `Long` sentinels beat `null` bounds here? What breaks with `Int` values at the edges?
What if equal values are allowed on one side only — adjust the comparison.
Recover the BST from a pre-order traversal.

items.q: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
shortAnswer: Return the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` as descendants, where a node is its own descendant.
Recurse and return what was found: a node equal to `p` or `q` returns itself; a node finding both targets is the LCA.
This assumes both nodes are present. If not, use a two-pass count instead. Otherwise, it's one O(n) pass with O(height) recursion.
items.prompt:
Given a binary tree and two node references `p` and `q` (both guaranteed present), return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both as descendants (itself included).

Classic recursive divide: each node asks "does my left or right subtree contain a target?" A node is the LCA exactly when one target is in each side, or it *is* a target and the other is somewhere below it.
hints: Define the recursion by what it *returns*, not what it mutates: return the found target, or the LCA if one side found each.
If a node is `p` or `q`, it can only be the answer if the other is in its subtree — so return it upward.
For each node: if both children return non-null, this node is the LCA. If one returns non-null, pass it up. If neither, null.

code.caption: Recursive — O(n)

items.complexity: Time O(n) — visits each node once. Space O(height) recursion (O(n) worst case). Note this assumes both nodes are present; if that's not guaranteed you need the two-pass "count matches" variant.
followUps: What changes if `p` or `q` might be absent? (Count found nodes first, then LCA.)
Now `p` is guaranteed to be an ancestor of `q` — how much simpler does it get?
LCA in a *binary search tree* — why is the range check enough?

shortAnswer: Return the diameter of a binary tree — the longest path between any two nodes, in edges.
The diameter through a node is `leftHeight + rightHeight`; compute height recursively and update a captured best on the way up.
The pattern is height with a side effect — a single O(n) pass beats recomputing heights. Space is O(height) recursion.
items.prompt:
Given a binary tree, return its diameter: the length of the longest path between any two nodes (in edges).

The classic "height with a side effect" pattern: the diameter through a node is `leftHeight + rightHeight`, and the global answer is the max over all nodes. You compute height recursively and update the max on the way up.
hints: The longest path passes through some node and goes down into both its subtrees. How long is the path through a given node?
Path length through a node = height(left) + height(right). The answer is the max of that over all nodes.
Write `height(n)` returning max depth, but update a running `best = max(best, l + r)` inside it. Single O(n) pass.

code.caption: Height recursion with a side effect — O(n)

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each node visited once. Space O(height) recursion. The two-pass (compute all heights then re-scan) is a common but worse answer; a single pass with a captured max is the point.
followUps: Return the actual path (nodes) of the diameter, not just the length.
Diameter counting *nodes* vs *edges* — off-by-one discussion.
Longest path in a *weighted* tree.

items.q: Serialize and Deserialize a Binary Tree
shortAnswer: Encode a binary tree to a string and rebuild it, using any unambiguous format.
Pre-order with explicit null markers writes the tree in one pass, and deserializing consumes tokens in the same recursive order.
The encoding must be unambiguous — in-order alone isn't. Both directions are O(n); level-order also works and is what caches tend to use.
items.prompt:
Design `serialize(root): String` and `deserialize(data): TreeNode?` for a binary tree. Any unambiguous format is acceptable; standard is pre-order with null markers (`"1,2,null,null,3,4,null,null,5,null,null"`).

The interview value is the encoding discipline: pre-order plus null markers makes the string uniquely reconstructible, and the deserializer consumes the token stream in the same order. This is the file-format design question of tree interviews.
hints: In-order alone is ambiguous for a tree — you need something that fixes the structure. What does pre-order + explicit nulls give you?
Pre-order: node, then left subtree (fully, including its nulls), then right. A single pass writes it; a single pass reads it.
Deserialize with an index into the split tokens: read a token, if `"null"` return null, else build the node and recurse left then right. An `ArrayDeque` of tokens makes the recursion trivial.

code.caption: Pre-order with null markers

items.complexity: Time O(n) both ways. Space O(n) for the string and recursion stack. Level-order serialization also works and is what production caches tend to use — mention the trade-off.
followUps: Serialize to a more compact form (omit trailing nulls / use a length prefix).
Serialize a *BST* — can you drop the nulls entirely?
Why not use in-order + another traversal? What ambiguity remains?
